notes.b: Biodiversity (the variety of living things in an ecosystem) is not just nice to have. It supplies services people depend on, keeps ecosystems stable, and many people argue it has a value of its own.
points: Ecosystem services are the benefits people get from ecosystems. Provisioning services are the products we take: food (crops, fish and game), timber, fibre, clean water and medicines.

Many medicines come from organisms, for example penicillin from the mould Penicillium, and aspirin's forerunner from willow bark (salicin). Losing a species can mean losing a drug nobody has found yet.
Regulating services control natural processes: pollination of crops by insects, purification of water by wetlands and soil, and pest control by predators. Bogs, forests and the sea also store carbon.
Wetlands and bogs also give flood control, because they soak up rain and release it slowly instead of letting it rush into rivers.

Supporting services keep the system running, such as soil formation and nutrient cycling by decomposers (organisms that break down dead matter). Cultural services include recreation, tourism, education, heritage and wellbeing.

Resilience (ability to withstand change) is higher in an ecosystem with many species and much genetic diversity. If one species declines, others with similar roles can take its place, and some individuals are likely to survive a new disease or a change in climate.
Low-diversity systems, such as a single crop variety, can collapse from one disease, because every plant is equally vulnerable.

The ethical argument: many people argue that species have a right to exist regardless of their usefulness, and that this generation has a duty to pass on a living world to future generations. Extinction is permanent, so the loss can never be undone.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to name ecosystem services, so learn one example of each type: provisioning, regulating, supporting and cultural. When explaining resilience, say why: other species can take over a lost species' role.

notes.b: Species are lost mainly because of human activity. There are seven main causes, and each one has Irish examples worth knowing.
points: Habitat loss and fragmentation is the biggest cause. Land is drained, built on, cut, or converted to intensive farming or plantation forestry. Irish examples: drainage and cutting of raised bogs, drainage of wet grassland, and removal of hedgerows.
Fragmentation (breaking habitat into pieces) leaves small, isolated patches that support only small populations, which are more easily wiped out by predators, disease or chance.

Agricultural intensification means earlier and more frequent mowing for silage (grass cut and stored as animal feed), reseeding with a few grass species, and more fertiliser. These reduce the variety of wild plants and destroy the nests of ground-nesting birds such as the curlew and the corncrake.

Pollution: excess nitrogen and phosphorus from fertiliser, slurry and sewage cause eutrophication (nutrient overload) of rivers and lakes. Silt from drainage, forestry and land works smothers river beds, and pesticides harm insects and their predators.

Invasive species are non-native species introduced by people that spread and harm native species and ecosystems, often because they have no natural predators or diseases in their new home. Irish examples: grey squirrel, zebra mussel and Rhododendron ponticum.
Overexploitation is harvesting faster than a population can replace itself, for example overfishing, peat extraction and over-collection.
Climate change forces species to shift their range or the timing of their life cycles. Cold-adapted species, and those in fragmented habitats, cannot always move far enough.
Disease: new pathogens (disease-causing organisms) spread by trade. Ash dieback, a fungal disease recorded in Ireland in 2012, is killing ash trees in hedgerows and woodland.
notes.tip: When asked for causes, give the cause and a specific Irish example for each, such as drained raised bogs for habitat loss or the grey squirrel for invasive species. Do not call every non-native species invasive: invasive means it spreads and causes harm.

notes.b: Raised bogs are one of Ireland's most distinctive habitats and one of its most damaged. They show clearly how one habitat can matter environmentally, economically, socially and culturally.
points: Raised bogs are dome-shaped peatlands, mainly in the Irish midlands, formed over thousands of years as Sphagnum moss grew over waterlogged ground. They are wet, acidic and low in nutrients.

Because conditions are so harsh, raised bogs support specialised species: Sphagnum mosses, sundews (insect-eating plants), bog cotton and heather, and animals such as the curlew, the red grouse and the Irish hare.
Loss came from centuries of hand turf cutting, then large-scale industrial peat extraction for fuel and horticulture in the twentieth century, plus drainage for farming and forestry.
As a result, less than about 1% of the original raised bog area is still active raised bog, meaning bog that is still forming peat.
Environmental impacts: loss of a rare habitat and its specialised species; drained peat releases stored carbon; and loss of flood control and water purification.
Economic impacts: peat fuelled power stations and supported jobs in the midlands, so ending extraction cost jobs, while restoration can bring tourism and “green” jobs.

Social and cultural impacts: turf cutting for home fuel is a centuries-old rural tradition, and many families hold turbary (turf-cutting) rights. Bogs also preserve archaeology and are part of Irish heritage and literature.
notes.tip: If a question gives a news story about a bog, organise your answer under the four headings: environmental, economic, social and cultural. Use a bog example under each.

notes.b: Once the scale of bog loss was clear, the law and public bodies stepped in. The result protects species but affects people who rely on the bog, so it is a good example of a conservation trade-off.
points: Many raised bogs are protected as Special Areas of Conservation (SACs) under the EU Habitats Directive. Turf cutting on them is banned, and compensation is offered to turf cutters, which has been controversial.
Bord na Móna ended industrial peat harvesting in 2021. Drained bogs are being rewetted by blocking drains to raise the water table, so that Sphagnum can regrow.
For restoration: it protects species and stores carbon.
Against restoration: it removes a traditional right and a cheap fuel, so it needs compensation and local support to succeed.
notes.tip: A discuss question needs both sides. Give the benefit (species and carbon) and the cost (lost turf rights and cheap fuel), then say compensation and local support are what make it work.

notes.b: The curlew shows how several pressures acting together can push a once-common bird towards disappearing from Ireland. It also shows how targeted conservation work tries to reverse that.
points: The curlew is a large wading bird with a long, down-curved bill that breeds on bogs and wet grassland. It is now one of Ireland's most threatened breeding birds.
A national survey in 2015–2017 found only 138 breeding pairs in the Republic of Ireland, a decline of at least 96% since the 1980s. A 2021 survey found about 105 pairs, so the fall has continued.
Causes of the decline: loss and drainage of bogs and wet grassland; plantation forestry on breeding sites; intensive farming with early mowing; and predation of eggs and chicks by foxes and crows.
Predation is worse because small breeding areas are surrounded by forest and farmland that support many predators.

Conservation: the Curlew Conservation Programme, run by the National Parks and Wildlife Service (NPWS) since 2017, employs local nest-finders and works with farmers to protect nests, manage habitat and control predators. Electric fencing against foxes is one example.
notes.tip: The curlew is not extinct in Ireland: it still breeds in small numbers. Say it is critically low or one of the most threatened, and give both the cause list and the programme.

notes.b: The corncrake is a second bird lost mainly to changes in how farmland is managed. Its story shows how timing and direction of mowing can decide whether chicks survive.
points: The corncrake is a secretive grassland bird with a rasping call that was once heard across rural Ireland in summer. Its population has fallen by more than 96% since the 1970s.
It now breeds mainly in Co. Donegal (including offshore islands) and on the western coast of Mayo and Galway. It has not disappeared from Ireland.
Main cause: mechanised mowing of hay and silage during the nesting season destroys nests. Mowing from the edge of a field inwards traps the chicks in the centre, because they have nowhere to escape.
Conservation: farmers are paid to delay mowing until the chicks can fly, to mow from the centre of the field outwards so chicks can escape to the edges, and to leave tall vegetation as cover.
The Corncrake LIFE project, EU-funded and launched in 2022, uses payments based on results, so farmers are rewarded for the outcome for the birds.

Cultural impact of both birds: the sounds of the curlew and the corncrake are part of rural Irish life, folklore, music and place names, so their loss is felt as a cultural loss as well as an ecological one.
notes.tip: For the corncrake, link the cause to the fix: edge-inwards mowing traps chicks, so centre-outwards mowing and delayed mowing let them escape. This pairing is an easy way to show a practice and its benefit.

notes.h: Invasive species: grey squirrel and pine marten
notes.b: An invasive species is one that, once introduced, spreads and harms native species. The grey squirrel is Ireland's best-known example, and the pine marten shows how a native predator can help reverse the damage.
points: The grey squirrel was introduced from North America. The Irish population began with a few animals released in 1911 at Castle Forbes, Co. Longford. It spread across the eastern half of the island, and red squirrels declined where it arrived.
The grey squirrel is larger and competes with the red squirrel for food, because their niches (their roles and resource needs) overlap.
It carries squirrelpox virus, which does not harm grey squirrels but is usually fatal to red squirrels. It also damages trees by stripping their bark.

The native pine marten, protected under the Wildlife Act 1976, has recovered. Where pine martens are common, for example in the Irish midlands, grey squirrels have declined or disappeared and red squirrels have returned.
The heavier grey squirrel is more easily caught by the pine marten.
This shows how restoring a native predator can help a native species.
notes.tip: Do not say the grey squirrel kills red squirrels. It outcompetes them for food and spreads squirrelpox, which is what you should write when asked to explain its effects.

notes.h: Invasive species: zebra mussel and quagga mussel
notes.b: Invasive species are not only land animals. In Irish lakes and rivers the zebra mussel has changed whole food chains, and it has itself now been displaced by a newer invader.
points: The zebra mussel is a small freshwater mussel native to the Ponto-Caspian region, around the Black and Caspian Seas. It was first recorded in Ireland in Lough Derg on the Shannon in 1997, probably brought on boats.
It spreads attached to boat hulls and in bilge water (the water that collects in the bottom of a boat), which is how it moves between lakes.

The zebra mussel filters huge volumes of water, removing phytoplankton (microscopic algae), the base of the food chain. The water becomes clearer, but food for zooplankton (tiny animals) and young fish falls.
The zebra mussel smothers native mussels and blocks water-intake pipes, an economic cost.
The zebra mussel has itself been displaced in Lough Derg by a related invader, the quagga mussel, first recognised there in 2021. The quagga mussel is a separate species.
notes.tip: When asked for the effects of a named invasive species, give an ecological effect (less phytoplankton, so less food for zooplankton and young fish) and an economic one (blocked intake pipes). Remember the quagga mussel is a different species.

notes.b: A plant can be invasive too. Rhododendron ponticum was brought in as a garden shrub, but in Killarney it now threatens the native woodland.
points: Rhododendron ponticum is a shrub introduced to Killarney for ornamental planting in the nineteenth century. It forms dense thickets in the native oak woodlands of Killarney National Park.
Its evergreen leaves let very little light reach the woodland floor, so oak seedlings and ground plants cannot grow and the wood cannot regenerate (replace its old trees).
Clearing it by cutting and treating regrowth is slow and costly, and the work must be repeated.
notes.tip: Explain the mechanism: shade from evergreen leaves stops oak seedlings growing. Name Killarney National Park as your place.

notes.b: Ireland has other invasive species too, and because removal is so costly, the best approach is to stop them spreading in the first place.
points: Elodea canadensis (Canadian pondweed) is an invasive plant in fresh water.
Japanese knotweed spreads from small root fragments, which makes it hard to remove, and damages buildings and riverbanks.
Prevention is through biosecurity (measures that stop species being moved). An example is the “check, clean, dry” routine for boats and angling gear moved between waters.
Never release aquarium plants or pets into the wild, because they may establish and spread where they have no natural predators.

notes.b: Clean water is vital to freshwater life. Two cases show what happens when silt and excess nutrients get into Irish rivers and lakes.
points: The freshwater pearl mussel is a long-lived mussel of clean, fast-flowing rivers. Its larvae (glochidia) must attach to the gills of young native salmon or trout to develop, and the juveniles need clean, well-oxygenated gravel.
Silt and nutrient enrichment from drainage, forestry and farming clog the gravel. In many Irish rivers few or no young mussels survive, and populations consist only of old adults.
Its decline is also linked to the decline of salmon and trout, its hosts, because without them the larvae cannot develop.
Lough Neagh, in Northern Ireland and the largest lake on the island of Ireland, had a massive bloom of blue-green algae (cyanobacteria) in summer 2023.
The bloom was linked mainly to excess phosphorus from agriculture and wastewater built up over decades, along with warm, still weather and zebra mussels.
Impacts of the Lough Neagh bloom: toxic water unsafe for people, pets and livestock; harm to fish and birds; damage to the eel fishery and to tourism; and anger in local communities.
notes.tip: Say Lough Neagh is on the island of Ireland, not in the Republic. For the pearl mussel, link the cause (silt clogging gravel) to the effect (no young mussels, only old adults).

notes.h: Impacts of biodiversity loss: environmental and economic
notes.b: Biodiversity loss damages ecosystems and costs money. Each point below is paired with an example from the Irish case studies.
points: Environmental: food webs are disrupted when a species is lost, affecting its predators and prey. Ecosystem services such as pollination, water purification and flood control are lost, ecosystems become less resilient, and extinction is irreversible.

Environmental example: about one third of Ireland's wild bee species are threatened with extinction, mainly through loss of flowers and nesting sites. This threatens the pollination of wild plants and crops.
Economic: farming depends on pollinators and healthy soil, and fisheries and angling depend on clean rivers and lakes.
Tourism, for example at Killarney National Park, the Burren and the bogs, depends on landscapes and wildlife.
Invasive species cost money to control, for example clearing rhododendron or unblocking pipes fouled by zebra mussels. Polluted water also costs more to treat.
Conservation also has costs, including compensation to farmers and turf cutters and lost income from land use.
notes.tip: 'Discuss the impact' questions on a news story expect all four headings with an example for each. Take your examples from a case study, and include conservation costs as well as the costs of loss.

notes.h: Impacts of biodiversity loss: social and cultural
notes.b: Biodiversity loss also affects people's health, communities and identity. It can cause conflict, because both loss and the rules to prevent it can hit livelihoods.
points: Social: health and wellbeing benefit from access to nature. Polluted water threatens drinking supplies and recreation, for example on Lough Neagh.
Social conflict: communities that depend on fishing, farming or peat can lose their livelihoods either from biodiversity loss or from conservation rules, which causes conflict.
Cultural: species and landscapes are part of identity, heritage, folklore, music, literature and place names, for example the curlew, the corncrake and the bogs.
Traditional practices such as turf cutting are themselves cultural heritage, which is why some conservation measures are resisted.
notes.tip: Make the social point two-sided: livelihoods can be lost to biodiversity loss and to conservation rules. This is why compensation and local support come up in every conservation answer.

notes.b: Conservation means acting to protect nature. There are two broad approaches, depending on whether the species is protected where it lives or somewhere else.
points: Conservation is the protection, management and restoration of the natural environment to maintain biodiversity and prevent extinction, while allowing sustainable use.
In situ conservation (in the natural habitat) uses protected areas such as national parks. Killarney National Park was Ireland's first, in 1932.
Natura 2000 sites across the EU include Special Areas of Conservation (SACs) under the EU Habitats Directive (1992) and Special Protection Areas (SPAs) for birds under the EU Birds Directive (1979).
Species protection under the Wildlife Act 1976 made it illegal to kill or disturb protected species.
Habitat management and restoration: rewetting bogs; planting native trees and hedgerows; and controlling invasive species.
Farming for nature uses agri-environment schemes that pay farmers for results, such as species-rich meadows, for example in the Burren.
Species recovery programmes include the Curlew Conservation Programme and the Corncrake LIFE project.
Ex situ conservation (outside the natural habitat) uses seed banks, captive breeding and reintroduction, for example captive rearing of freshwater pearl mussels to release young mussels into rivers.
notes.tip: Define conservation, then describe one practice and its benefit. Name the type (in situ or ex situ) and give a specific Irish example, such as Killarney National Park or rewetting bogs.

notes.b: Laws and national plans set the direction for conservation, but individuals and communities also take part.
points: The All-Ireland Pollinator Plan, launched in 2015, asks councils, farmers, schools and gardeners to provide flowers and nesting sites for bees, for example by mowing road verges less often.
In May 2019 the Dáil declared a climate and biodiversity emergency, making Ireland the second country to do so.
The Citizens' Assembly on Biodiversity Loss reported in April 2023 with 159 recommendations.
Ireland's fourth National Biodiversity Action Plan covers 2023–2030.
The EU Nature Restoration Law, adopted in 2024, requires member states to restore damaged ecosystems.

Individuals can record species for citizen-science surveys (research that members of the public contribute to), for example through the National Biodiversity Data Centre. They can also garden for pollinators and avoid spreading invasive species.

notes.b: A discuss question wants both sides: where conservation has worked, and where it has fallen short. A balanced answer then reaches a conclusion.
points: Arguments for its effectiveness: protection has brought recoveries, for example the pine marten after 1976, with the return of red squirrels that followed.
Rewetting can restore bog habitat, and targeted payments have raised the breeding success of curlew and corncrake in some areas.
Protected areas keep the last strongholds of rare species.
Limits: declines continue, as curlew numbers fell further between 2015–17 and 2021. Designating a site is not enough without enforcement and management.
Schemes cost money and can conflict with the incomes and traditions of farmers, turf cutters and landowners.
Small, isolated populations may still be lost to predators, disease or chance. Restoration is slow: bogs take centuries to re-form.
Conclusion to model: conservation limits biodiversity loss when it has funding, enforcement and the support of the local people who manage the land.
notes.tip: Always give both the effectiveness arguments and the limits, then finish with the conclusion about funding, enforcement and local support.

notes.h: Exploring local ecosystems through news and local media
notes.b: The syllabus asks you to link what you learn to real, current stories about local ecosystems. Follow these steps to analyse a story.
points: 1. Find a current local story about a local ecosystem or species. Sources include local newspapers and radio, national news, the websites of the NPWS and the EPA (water quality), BirdWatch Ireland, the National Biodiversity Data Centre, and the county council's heritage or biodiversity officer.
2. Identify the ecosystem, the species affected, the cause, and the evidence, such as survey data, photographs or expert opinion.
3. Evaluate the source: who wrote it, whether it is based on data, whether it shows bias (for example from a campaign group or an industry body), and whether other sources agree.
4. Describe the impacts under the four headings: environmental, economic, social and cultural.
5. Assess what conservation is being done and whether it is likely to work.
6. Where possible, visit or survey the ecosystem to gather primary data (data you collect yourself).
notes.tip: Exams may give a news article as stimulus. Use the four impact headings and the evaluation of conservation to structure your answer.

keyTerms.definition: The protection, management and restoration of the natural environment to maintain biodiversity and prevent extinction, while allowing sustainable use.
The benefits people get from ecosystems, grouped as provisioning, regulating, supporting and cultural services.
The ability of an ecosystem to remain stable or recover after change, which is higher where there are many species and much genetic diversity.
The breaking up of a habitat into small, isolated patches that support only small populations.
Farming practices such as earlier mowing, reseeding and more fertiliser that reduce wild plant variety and destroy wildlife habitat.
A non-native species introduced by people that spreads and harms native species and ecosystems.
Harvesting a population faster than it can replace itself.
Enrichment of a lake or river with nutrients, such as nitrogen and phosphorus, which can lead to algal blooms.
A dome-shaped, wet, acidic and nutrient-poor peatland formed as Sphagnum moss grows over waterlogged ground.
The traditional right to cut turf for fuel on a bog.
Blocking drains on a drained bog to raise the water table so that Sphagnum can regrow.
A site protected under the EU Habitats Directive, forming part of the Natura 2000 network.
A site protected under the EU Birds Directive for birds, forming part of the Natura 2000 network.
Conservation of species in their natural habitat, e.g. through protected areas.
Conservation of species outside their natural habitat, e.g. through seed banks, captive breeding and reintroduction.
The larvae of the freshwater pearl mussel, which must attach to the gills of young salmon or trout to develop.
Scientific surveys in which members of the public record species and report their observations.
Measures, such as cleaning boats and gear between waters, that stop invasive species from spreading.

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by an invasive species and describe the impact of one named invasive species on an Irish ecosystem.
questions.model: An invasive species is a non-native species introduced by people that spreads and harms native species and ecosystems, often because it has no natural predators or diseases in its new home. It competes with the red squirrel for food because their niches overlap, and it carries squirrelpox virus, which is usually fatal to red squirrels. Red squirrels have declined where grey squirrels have arrived. Alternatively, the zebra mussel filters out phytoplankton, reduces food for zooplankton, smothers native mussels and blocks water-intake pipes in Lough Derg.

questions.prompt: Discuss the impact of the loss of raised bogs in Ireland and the role of conservation in limiting this loss.

questions.prompt: The breeding curlew population in Ireland has declined by at least 96% since the 1980s. Suggest reasons for this decline and describe how conservation can help.
questions.model: Reasons for the decline include loss and drainage of bogs and wet grassland, plantation forestry on breeding sites, intensive farming with early mowing, and predation of eggs and chicks by foxes and crows, which is worse because small breeding areas are surrounded by predator-rich forest and farmland.
